 Who Dropped the Ball on County’s Ballots? Election Day Issues Spark Calls for Accountability
 New York is the only state in the U.S. where political parties – rather than elected or appointed officials – nominate state and local election administrators. Westchester’s Board of Elections commissioners, Tajian Nelson and Douglas Colety, are among the highest-paid county employees. 
 By Chris Marshall 
 Published on 
 November 21, 2026 
 Westchester County Board of Elections commissioners Tajian Nelson and Douglas Colety. Photo courtesy of Westchester County Legislators Instagram 
 State and county officials have pledged to investigate the failure of voting machines in Westchester County on Election Day and hold those responsible accountable.
 The state Board of Elections said it plans to “undertake a full and careful bipartisan review of the circumstances leading up to and occurring on Election Day. Findings will be shared with the public to provide accountability and identify corrective actions.”
 County Executive Ken Jenkins promised the same.
 “While the Board of Elections does not report to me, my responsibility is to look out for the people of Westchester County,” Jenkins said, “And I share their anger and frustration over what occurred.”
 On Election Day, voting machines around the county failed to scan ballots, requiring those ballots to be tallied by hand and delaying final results for four days. 
 Initial explanations evolved from an issue involving paper thickness to software issues to printing problems. Weeks after the polls closed, specific details remain unclear – as well as what actions will be taken to prevent future gaffes. 
 The extended vote-counting process did not affect any Westchester races, which had convincing enough margins to be decided on Election Night. But the ballot issues did spark countywide questions, and national speculation, about what went wrong in Westchester.
 “This is not about politics or pointing fingers,” Jenkins said. “It is about accountability, transparency, and ensuring public confidence in our election process. The voters deserve answers, but – and maybe more importantly – they deserve better and I intend to make sure they get it.”
 County Executive Blames Election-Day Debacle on ‘Printer Problem,’ Assures All Votes Will Be Counted Securely 
 New York is the only state in the U.S. where political parties – rather than elected or appointed officials – nominate state and local election administrators. 
 In every New York county, one Democratic and one Republican commissioner of elections are recommended by their respective political party and appointed by the Board of Legislators for a term of four years. 
 Westchester County’s Board of Elections commissioners, Democrat Tajian Nelson and Republican Douglas Colety, are two of the highest-paid county employees, both with salaries over $200,000. 
 Nelson and Colety oversee 106 employees, including 10 voting machine technicians, a pair of supervising voting machine technicians, and eight directors of technical services. According to the county’s operating budget, the board’s expenditures for 2026 were budgeted at $28.1 million.
 Among their operational duties are ballot scanners and ballot materials and supplies. The malfunction of those basic voting instruments led to the cascade of problems that affected polling locations countywide.
 Colety and Nelson and the state Board of Elections have not responded to repeated requests by The Rye Record for comment. The commissioners and board have said they were busy scanning ballots, reconciling results, canvassing, and certifying the results.
 Colety, a White Plains resident, has been the Republican commissioner of the county board since 2011, and was previously chairman of the New Rochelle Republican City Committee for 14 years. His deputy commissioner, Christine Sculti, was the Republican candidate running against Jenkins for county executive in a 2025 special election.
 Nelson, from Pelham, was unanimously selected by the Westchester County Democratic Party’s Executive Committee in 2022, making her the first Black woman to serve as a commissioner on the county Board of Elections. She replaced Reginald LaFayette, who died in office after holding the role from 1999 to 2022.
 The party had apparently been pleased with Nelson’s work. She was elected vice-chairwoman of the Westchester County Democratic Committee on Oct. 7, four weeks before midterm elections.
 County elections officials appear to be highly independent of the state. 
 The state Board of Elections website says, “Many core election administration functions such as voter registration list maintenance, poll site planning, voting technology procurement, issuance of absentee ballots, review of absentee and affidavit ballots, and post-election canvassing are in the hands of the local Boards rather than being performed or supervised by the State Board.”
 This is not the first time a local election board has run into ballot issues. In June 2020, the Monroe County Board of Elections left a Democratic state Senate candidate’s name off some primary ballots. A year later, a well-publicized results tabulation error by the New York City Board of Elections prompted the state Senate Elections Committee to hold hearings, collecting testimony from voters, poll workers, elections officials, and scholars.
 In November 2021, the committee published a report of its findings : “The State Board does not assert day-to-day supervisory authority over local County Boards’ management decisions, and indeed recently asserted that it ‘does not investigate local boards.’”
 The report called for structural reforms of county boards, changes to the relationship between state and local boards, and operational changes, including reforming the selection process, qualifications, and accountability structure for elections commissioners.
 In 2023, the Senate proposed stricter requirements and annual training for commissioners, but the state Assembly never brought it to the floor.
 While the state board does not oversee county boards directly, one of its key responsibilities is to provide help when needed. So, after consulting with Nelson and Colety during the aftermath of Election Day, the state board sent a team of 20 people from Albany to Ardsley, where executives and staff joined the counting efforts at the Westchester County Board of Elections office.
 County staff started counting emergency ballots at 11 a.m. the morning after Election Day. A total of 15,467 emergency ballots were scanned on Wednesday, Nov. 4. The next day, 63,980 more were scanned.
 Update: As Week-Long Vote-Counting Process Concludes, County Executive Ken Jenkins Denies Blame for Balloting Gaffe 
 The state board said when it arrived on Nov. 5, roughly 149,000 emergency ballots still needed to be scanned. After implementing “workflow improvements that expedited the process,” the counting was completed by 8:45 p.m. Friday.
 “The response combined technical assistance, additional scanning equipment, increased staffing, and changes to the processing workflow to help Westchester complete this substantial task while maintaining ballot security and bipartisan oversight,” the state board said in a statement.
 By working alongside the Suffolk County Board of Elections and Clear Ballot, a post-election auditing company, the state board got nine additional scanning stations up and running, complementing the three scanners Westchester was initially using.
 While the wait for final election results took days, an explanation for the county’s issues has taken much longer. Jenkins pledges to stay on top of the matter and demand answers. 
 “What happened on Election Day in Westchester County remains completely unacceptable,” Jenkins said. “We are a county of more than one million residents, and voters deserve to have complete confidence in the integrity, security, and reliability of our election system.
 “Following the official certification of the election results, I will convene a bipartisan review to thoroughly examine the decisions, actions, and failures that led to this debacle. This review will focus on determining what went wrong, where accountability lies, and what steps must be taken to ensure that a failure of this magnitude never happens again.”
